narrative:
The model predicts you have a 17% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most strongly influenced this prediction were your number of past class failures, your desire to pursue higher education, and your mother's job. Surprisingly, having no previous failures was the strongest element pulling the prediction toward passing. Your clear ambition to continue studying beyond high school also pushed the outcome in a positive direction. However, your mother's occupation as a teacher worked against these advantages and became the main reason the model still saw a risk of failure.

Because the positive influences from your clean record and strong educational goals were not quite enough to overcome the negative signal coming from your family background, the overall prediction tipped toward failure. This combination explains why remedial courses are now mandatory.

To improve, focus on turning your ambition into consistent daily study habits. Although you currently study less than two hours per week—while most students who passed spend two to five hours—building a regular routine could close the gap. Reducing your eight absences, which is more than double the average of students who succeeded, would also help demonstrate your commitment and strengthen your final performance.
